comparison: Perfect agreement on implementation claims (C4, C5, C20, C23, C25). Both evaluations find the OpenSpliceAI implementation well-documented and functional. OpenEval cites architectural diagrams and experimental validation; peer reviewers confirm code quality and documentation through hands-on testing.

Significant disagreement on calibration claims (C19, C53-C56). OpenEval finds claims supported but notes 'slight' improvements and limited practical impact. Peer Reviewer 1 raises substantial concerns about inadequate discussion of calibration limitations, noting dataset-specificity issues that 'could lead to serious errors.' Evaluation types differ: SUPPORTED vs UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on ensemble methodology and N-padding artifact (C73-C75). Both accept these technical details without challenge. OpenEval notes the practical impact of the N-padding bias is unclear; peer reviewers accept it as part of model characterization.
Complete agreement on biological background claims (C10-C13). Both recognize these as well-established facts supported by citations, serving as foundational context rather than novel findings.

Strong agreement on computational performance claims (C6, C7, C17, C18, C35-C37, C63-C64). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of benchmarking data; peer reviewers confirm 'convincing evidence' of improved computational efficiency. Peer review includes technical explanation claims (C63-C64) that OpenEval addresses separately in R11.

Agreement on transfer learning claims (C50-C52, C70). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of training curves and convergence benefits; peer reviewers note that 'pre-training on other species helps improve performance.' Peer review also includes reverse transfer learning claims (C71-C72) that OpenEval addresses separately in R10.

Agreement on motivation and background claims (C2, C3, C15, C16). Both accept framework compatibility issues and human-centric training limitations as valid motivation. OpenEval validates limitation claims through cross-species experiments; peer reviewers accept these as established context. Peer review also includes C1 and C14 that OpenEval addresses in R13.

Strong agreement on model equivalence claims (C8, C9, C57-C62). OpenEval cites ISM experiments, correlation analyses, and cryptic splicing validation; peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence' that models match original's understanding of non-local mutation effects. Peer review groups these with training variability claims (C21-C22, C30-C34) that OpenEval addresses separately.

Agreement on cross-species training performance (C38, C39, C44-C47). OpenEval provides detailed analysis noting large gains in distant species; peer reviewers confirm 'strong performance on non-human model species.' Peer review also includes interpretation claims (C24, C68-C69) that OpenEval addresses in R9. OpenEval separately evaluates paralog removal methodology (C40-C43) in context of R5.

Agreement on training procedure claims (C26-C29). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of OSAIMANE training with performance metrics; peer reviewers implicitly accept methodological details. OpenEval also evaluates performance improvement claims (C30-C34) that peer review addresses in R3.

Agreement on neural network variability principles (C65-C67). Both recognize these as established knowledge providing methodological context. OpenEval also addresses training variability claims (C21-C22) that peer review includes in R3.

Agreement on paralog removal methodology (C40-C43). OpenEval evaluates this as part of cross-species training experiments; peer reviewers accept the methodology without challenge as part of experimental design.
Agreement on transfer learning background (C48-C49). Both recognize these as established knowledge supported by citations, providing rationale for experiments rather than novel findings.

Agreement on cross-species performance interpretation (C24, C68-C69). OpenEval notes phylogenetic distance relationship is reasonable but alternative explanations not fully explored; peer reviewers accept these summary claims as part of overall cross-species results without specific challenge.

Agreement on reverse transfer learning (C71-C72). OpenEval characterizes this as a valuable negative result showing limits of transfer learning; peer reviewers accept it as part of transfer learning demonstration without specific comment.
Agreement on SpliceAI background (C1, C14). Both recognize these as established facts from original SpliceAI work, accepted as foundational context for the manuscript.

Agreement on technical performance explanations (C63-C64). OpenEval notes attribution to PyTorch advantages is reasonable inference not directly validated; peer reviewers accept these as part of computational efficiency evidence without specific challenge to the technical explanation.

Agreement on OSAIMANE performance claims (C30-C34). OpenEval notes improvements are modest but statistically meaningful; peer reviewers accept model equivalence evidence that includes these performance metrics without challenging the magnitude of improvements.

Agreement on training variability principles (C21-C22). OpenEval recognizes these as well-established principles; peer reviewers implicitly accept them as part of the evidence for model equivalence and ensemble methodology.
